key_concepts.title: Volleyball role demands are phase-specific
key_concepts.summary: A role profile should describe responsibilities separately for serve receive, offense, block, floor defense, and transition. The same player may have a primary responsibility in one phase and a support responsibility in another.
key_concepts.backend_use: Store phase responsibility maps rather than a single free-text role description.

key_concepts.title: Legal court position is different from specialized role
key_concepts.summary: All players rotate through court zones, but teams assign specialized roles such as setter, libero, middle, outside, opposite, defensive specialist, and serving specialist. Role logic must still respect front-row/back-row, attack-line, substitution, and libero rules.
key_concepts.backend_use: Separate role tags from rotation/legal-position constraints in retrieval.

key_concepts.title: The setter is the offense organizer
key_concepts.summary: The setter usually owns the second contact, converts pass quality into hittable options, controls tempo, calls or signals plays, manages matchups, and decides when to involve each attacker or ask for help.
key_concepts.backend_use: Setter plans should combine technical setting, decision-making, communication, and movement-to-ball work.

key_concepts.title: The outside hitter is usually the all-around pin and high-ball outlet
key_concepts.summary: Outside hitters often combine serve-receive passing, left-side attacking, back-row defense, emergency high-ball attacking, and left-side blocking. Their role requires tolerance for imperfect sets and heavy scoring pressure.
key_concepts.backend_use: Outside hitter profiles should prioritize passing plus out-of-system attack before advanced combination play.

key_concepts.title: The opposite provides right-side attack and block balance
key_concepts.summary: Opposites play opposite the setter in many systems, attack from the right side, often block the opponent's outside hitter, may carry back-row attack load, and may or may not receive serve depending on level and roster.
key_concepts.backend_use: Opposite records should allow both receive and non-receive variants.

key_concepts.title: The middle blocker is a speed, read, and net-control role
key_concepts.summary: Middle blockers must read pass quality and setter cues, close blocks across the net, handle overpasses, attack first-tempo balls, and transition rapidly from block landing into approach availability.
key_concepts.backend_use: Middle blocker plans should pair fast read-block footwork with quick-attack timing and landing capacity.

key_concepts.title: The libero anchors serve receive and floor defense
key_concepts.summary: The libero is a back-row specialist with unique replacement rules and attack/block restrictions. Coaching priorities include serve-receive range, digging, free-ball handling, out-of-system second-ball help, communication, and defensive leadership.
key_concepts.backend_use: Libero records should include both tactical leadership and legal restrictions.

key_concepts.title: A defensive specialist is a back-row substitution role, not the libero rule category
key_concepts.summary: A defensive specialist usually enters through normal substitutions to improve serve receive, digging, serving, or back-row control. Unlike a libero, the defensive specialist is not defined by special libero replacement privileges or the same attack/block restrictions.
key_concepts.backend_use: Treat defensive specialist as a tactical substitute role with normal substitution costs and optional serving.

key_concepts.title: A serving specialist is a short-exposure pressure role
key_concepts.summary: Serving specialists enter primarily to create serve pressure, target a passer, change serve type, or manage a weak server's rotation. Their value depends on serve efficiency, substitution rules, and ability to defend immediately after serving if they remain in the rally.
key_concepts.backend_use: Serving specialist records should include high-pressure routine, serve target selection, and cold-entry readiness.

key_concepts.title: Blocking and floor defense are one system
key_concepts.summary: The block may stop the attack outright or channel it to assigned defenders. Front-row players must coordinate hand position and timing with the floor defense behind them.
key_concepts.backend_use: Block drills should specify the defender locations the block is protecting or conceding.

key_concepts.title: Role load clusters into jumping, overhead swings, and low defensive posture
key_concepts.summary: Hitters and middles carry more jump, landing, block, and swing load; setters carry repeated movement-to-second-ball and jump-setting/blocking load; liberos and defensive specialists carry low-stance, reaction, receive, dig, and dive load; serving specialists carry concentrated overhead serve exposure and cold-entry stress.
key_concepts.backend_use: Physical demand rules should be role-weighted rather than one generic volleyball conditioning template.

technical_models.title: Role phase responsibility matrix
technical_models.description: Map each role to primary and secondary actions in serve receive, offense, block, defense, and transition.

setter.serve_receive: Usually releases from receive pattern to setting target; may pass only in emergency or beginner systems.
setter.offense: Owns second contact, tempo, set selection, play calls, attacker confidence, and matchup exploitation.
setter.block: Front-row setter blocks in right-front or assigned zone; must handle setter dump decisions when opponent setter is front row.
setter.defense: Back-row setter defends assigned zone after serve; front-row setter covers tips/dumps when not blocking.
setter.transition: Moves from dig/block-cover into setting position or calls help when first contact removes access.

outside_hitter.serve_receive: Common primary passer with libero and/or defensive specialist; manages seams and prepares full approach after pass.
outside_hitter.offense: Primary left-side attacker, high-ball outlet, out-of-system scorer, back-row option at advanced levels.
outside_hitter.block: Blocks opponent right-side attacker or assigned pin; sets outside edge and line/cross-court plan.
outside_hitter.defense: Defends left-back or perimeter zone by system; covers tips, rolls, and cross-court lanes.
outside_hitter.transition: Changes from pass/dig/block-cover into approach quickly, often on imperfect or high sets.

opposite.serve_receive: May be hidden from receive or used as a passer depending on level, system, and roster.
opposite.offense: Right-side front-row attacker, back-row right-side option in advanced systems, emergency set option when setter digs first ball.
opposite.block: Frequently blocks the opponent outside hitter, so lateral speed, hand discipline, and matchup scouting matter.
opposite.defense: Defends right-back or assigned perimeter zone; may protect line or cross-court behind block scheme.
opposite.transition: Switches from blocking left-side attacks into right-side approach or from right-back defense into pipe/D-ball routes.

middle_blocker.serve_receive: Usually limited receive role after beginner stages; prepares for quick approach if pass quality allows.
middle_blocker.offense: First-tempo quick attacker, slide option in some systems, overpass finisher, decoy to hold opposing middle.
middle_blocker.block: Central read blocker responsible for first-tempo threat and closing to both pins.
middle_blocker.defense: Front-row net defender; when back row, often replaced by libero, but may defend if roster or rules require.
middle_blocker.transition: Must land, turn, separate from net, and become available for quick or cover responsibility within a short time window.

libero.serve_receive: Primary passer with the largest stable receive range the roster can support.
libero.offense: Cannot be a front-row attacker; provides out-of-system second-ball help and legal back-row setting choices.
libero.block: Does not block or attempt to block under FIVB rules.
libero.defense: Back-row defensive organizer, dig specialist, free-ball controller, and communication leader.
libero.transition: After first contact, covers attacker, handles second ball if setter defends, and resets team shape.

defensive_specialist.serve_receive: Substitution-based passer for a front-row specialist or weaker receiver; may cover a seam or targeted server lane.
defensive_specialist.offense: Usually limited attacking role but can back-row attack or emergency set if legal and trained.
defensive_specialist.block: Normally not used for front-row blocking, unless roster/substitution pattern requires it.
defensive_specialist.defense: Back-row dig, floor defense, serve receive, and ball-control stabilizer.
defensive_specialist.transition: Converts dig/pass into coverage, out-of-system setting help, or controlled free-ball decisions.

serving_specialist.serve_receive: Usually not inserted to receive unless also a defensive specialist.
serving_specialist.offense: Minimal offensive role; may need free-ball or emergency second contact if rally continues.
serving_specialist.block: Not a primary block role unless the serving substitution remains through front-row rotations.
serving_specialist.defense: Must be ready to defend immediately after serve, usually in right-back or assigned post-serve base.
serving_specialist.transition: Primary transition is serve-to-defense: finish serve, recover into base, read first opponent contact.

technical_models.title: Defensive read sequence
sequence: Know opponent rotation and whether the opposing setter is front row or back row.
Read pass quality because it constrains which attackers and tempos are realistic.
Read setter body, jump, contact point, and tendency.
Read hitter approach line, speed, shoulder, and hand.
Execute the block or floor defensive assignment that matches the team plan.
technical_models.backend_use: Use as a shared match-IQ progression and specialize examples by role.

technical_models.title: Serve receive to attack connection
technical_models.description: The passer's job is not finished at first contact. Outside hitters and opposites who pass must recover into an approach lane, middles must time quick availability based on pass quality, and the setter must convert the pass into the best available attack option.
technical_models.backend_use: Serve-receive drills for hitters should include pass-plus-approach and pass-plus-coverage constraints.

technical_models.title: Setter decision model
decision_steps: Can the setter take the second contact with balance and legal contact quality?
What attacker options are available from pass location and tempo?
Which attacker has the best matchup, hot hand, or tactical advantage?
Will a faster tempo reduce blocker read time without lowering set quality?
If the setter cannot set, who has the cleanest second-ball responsibility?
technical_models.backend_use: Create setter constraints that train movement, neutral body shape, communication, and set selection together.

technical_models.title: Blocker read-to-close model
sequence: Start in balanced ready position with peripheral awareness.
Identify likely setter options from pass quality.
Track setter release and attacker approach.
Move with efficient shuffle, crossover, or swing-block pattern based on distance.
Jump on time, press hands into the opponent's space without early interference, land balanced, and transition.
technical_models.backend_use: Block progressions should not isolate jump height from reading, footwork, hand shape, and landing.

technical_models.title: Role development stages

stages.beginner: Broad volleyball literacy first: serve, pass, set, attack approach basics, safe landing, simple base defense, communication, and rotation understanding.
stages.intermediate: Position-specific priority work layered onto all-around skills: serve-receive lanes, set tempo, role-specific block assignments, transition responsibilities, and low-error tactical choices.
stages.advanced: Scouting-driven specialization: rotation matchups, serve targeting, attacker tendency reads, opponent setter patterns, tempo variation, role-specific load management, and pressure routines.

technical_models.backend_use: Avoid early over-specialization in beginner plans; increase role specificity as the athlete's skill and game model mature.

tactical_rules.rule: Under FIVB rules, the libero is restricted to back-row play, may not complete an attack hit when the ball is entirely above the net, may not block or attempt to block, and has limits on front-zone overhand setting that leads to an above-net attack.
tactical_rules.backend_response: When prescribing libero offensive tasks, use legal back-row setting, forearm set options, emergency second-ball control, and coverage rather than front-row attacking or blocking.

tactical_rules.rule: Back-row players may attack above net height only when takeoff is behind the attack line; this affects setter dumps, opposite D-ball routes, outside pipe routes, and DS emergency attacking.
tactical_rules.backend_response: Attach attack-line constraints to back-row attack drills and block attempts.

tactical_rules.rule: In serve receive, the setter should release to the setting target when possible; if the setter takes first contact or cannot reach second contact cleanly, the pre-assigned help setter should take the ball.
tactical_rules.backend_response: Team drills should define emergency second-contact roles, commonly libero, right-back, or nearest non-attacking player.

tactical_rules.rule: The outside hitter should be trained as a reliable high-ball and imperfect-pass outlet because left-side high sets remain available when the pass pulls the setter off the net.
tactical_rules.backend_response: Outside hitter development should include out-of-system footwork, shot selection, block tooling, and error management.

tactical_rules.rule: Opposites often face the opponent's highest-volume outside attack, so their block plan must define line responsibility, cross-court channeling, hand discipline, and setter-front-row awareness.
tactical_rules.backend_response: Opposite training should include pin blocking and serve-to-block transition, not only attacking.

tactical_rules.rule: The middle blocker should use pass quality as an early cue: tight passes require overpass and setter-dump readiness, while off-net passes usually reduce quick-middle threat and shift attention to pins.
tactical_rules.backend_response: Middle blocker read drills should start with varied pass quality rather than predictable coach tosses only.

tactical_rules.rule: A high-range libero can absorb more court in serve receive, which can protect an outside hitter's approach or hide a weaker passer.
tactical_rules.backend_response: Serve-receive system recommendations should vary court-coverage load by libero range and outside hitter passing skill.

tactical_rules.rule: A defensive specialist improves back-row ball control but generally uses normal substitutions, so the tactical value must exceed the substitution and rotation cost.
tactical_rules.backend_response: Use DS recommendations when a team needs serve receive/dig stability and has substitution capacity.

tactical_rules.rule: A serving specialist is justified when the expected serve pressure, target matchup, or tactical change outweighs the risk of service error and the substitution cost.
tactical_rules.backend_response: Serving specialist drills should track both aces/poor passes forced and missed serves under cold-entry pressure.

tactical_rules.rule: The block and floor defense should agree what space is taken away and what space is intentionally defended.
tactical_rules.backend_response: Pair every blocking task with defender location, read, and dig target.

primary_demands: repeated short accelerations to second contact
jump setting and occasional front-row blocking
trunk control while moving and setting
physical_demands.load_notes: Setter load is more cognitive and movement-to-ball dense than maximal swing dense. Front-row setters still need block and landing preparation.
Outside hitters often combine the largest all-around skill load: pass, attack, block, defend, and transition under pressure.
Opposite physical load varies by system: some are protected from serve receive and carry more attack/block load, while others pass and play all-around.

primary_demands: rapid lateral movement along the net
physical_demands.load_notes: Middles have highly concentrated net load and must repeatedly jump, land, change direction, and become attack-available in short windows.
Libero load is lower in jumps but high in low posture, reaction, pass/dig contacts, and repeated floor-defense actions.

primary_demands: serving if substitution pattern includes serve
physical_demands.load_notes: A defensive specialist may play fewer rallies but must execute immediately with limited rhythm; warm-up and readiness routines matter.

physical_qualities: calf/Achilles stiffness for jump serve variants
physical_demands.load_notes: Serving specialists need low-volume but high-quality serving under pressure; the stress is less total workload and more precision on demand.

injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Net play, block/attack landings, and foot contact under the net increase acute ankle sprain risk, especially for frequent jumpers.
mitigation: teach vertical, controlled landings
progress block footwork before maximal jumps
include balance/proprioception work
consider external ankle support for athletes with sprain history

injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: High jump and landing volume, hard surfaces, spike approach mechanics, landing knee flexion/valgus stress, and large jumping ability can contribute to anterior knee pain and patellar tendinopathy.
mitigation: monitor jump volume and pain trend
build hip/thigh/landing capacity
use progressive plyometrics
avoid sudden increases in approach/block jumps
modify load when tendon symptoms rise

injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Repeated spiking, serving, and overhead contacts can overload rotator cuff, scapular stabilizers, and the shoulder girdle; spiking volume, scapular control, core stability, and rotational strength balance matter.
mitigation: track weekly swing and serve volume
train scapular stabilization and rotator cuff endurance
include posterior shoulder mobility as appropriate
build trunk power transfer
reduce spikes/serves during symptoms

injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Blocks, digs, awkward hand contacts, and setting volume can stress fingers, thumbs, and wrists.
mitigation: teach strong but relaxed hand shape
progress hard-driven dig volume
use taping or support when clinically indicated
avoid high-velocity blocking/digging volume in unprepared beginners

injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Serving, attacking, blocking reach, and repeated extension/rotation can irritate the low back; persistent extension-related back pain in young athletes warrants evaluation.
mitigation: build trunk strength and hip mobility
manage serving/attacking spikes
avoid forcing lumbar extension for power
refer persistent limiting back pain to qualified medical care

injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Repeated digs, sprawls, dives, rolls, and low defensive posture can stress wrists, shoulders, hips, knees, and low back even with low jump load.
mitigation: teach progressive floor skills
condition low-stance endurance
rotate high-volume digging drills
monitor wrist/shoulder soreness
include mobility and trunk control

injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: A player entering cold for a high-pressure serve may spike shoulder, trunk, calf, or Achilles stress if warm-up and routine are poor.
mitigation: use a repeatable bench-to-serve readiness routine
keep low-dose serving preparation available
match serve type to physical readiness
train serve-to-defense recovery

training_implications.implication: Beginners should not be locked too early into narrow roles. They need serve, pass, set, attack approach, basic block footwork, defensive base, safe landing, communication, and rotation literacy before deep specialization.
training_implications.backend_use: Beginner role plans should include 60-80 percent shared volleyball fundamentals and 20-40 percent role emphasis.

training_implications.implication: Setter development should progress from footwork-to-target, balanced hand setting, and simple high-ball choices to tempo variation, jump setting, matchup decisions, emergency help calls, and leadership under pressure.
training_implications.backend_use: Setter workouts should pair technical setting with decision constraints rather than static target reps only.

training_implications.implication: Outside hitters should first become stable passers and high-ball attackers, then add shot range, block tooling, seam responsibility, back-row defense, and advanced pipe/out-of-system attack.
training_implications.backend_use: Outside hitter drills should often require pass-to-approach or dig-to-transition, not isolated hitting only.

training_implications.implication: Opposite training should blend right-side attacking with blocking the opponent's outside hitter. At advanced levels, add back-row D-ball timing, setter-out first-ball emergency setting/attacking, and matchup serving patterns.
training_implications.backend_use: Opposite plans should expose both attack and block demands every week.

training_implications.implication: Middle blockers should progress from landing, block footwork, and simple quick timing to pass-quality reads, overpass decisions, slide/tempo options, commit/read-block choices, and fast block-to-attack transition.
training_implications.backend_use: Middle sessions should limit maximal jump volume until the athlete can read, move, land, and transition safely.

training_implications.implication: Libero development should move from platform control, serve-receive angles, and basic digging to large-area receive, seam leadership, tactical baiting, out-of-system setting, attacker coverage, and opponent tendency reads.
training_implications.backend_use: Libero plans should include communication and scanning tasks, not just passing reps.

training_implications.implication: Defensive specialists need libero-like passing and digging skills plus substitution readiness, serving consistency, and the flexibility to enter in different back-row patterns.
training_implications.backend_use: DS drills should include cold-entry serve receive, targeted-server pressure, and immediate communication with established passers.

training_implications.implication: Serving specialists should develop a primary high-confidence serve, a target plan, a pressure routine, and serve-to-defense recovery. Advanced players can add serve-type variation and scouting-based target decisions.
training_implications.backend_use: Track serve outcome quality under pressure: error, in-system pass allowed, out-of-system pass forced, ace/free-ball, and tactical target hit.

training_implications.implication: Volleyball S&C should include universal warm-up, landing mechanics, ankle balance, hip/trunk strength, shoulder/scapular durability, and mobility, then weight jump/overhead/low-stance loads by role.
training_implications.backend_use: Use role demand tags to adjust plyometric volume, shoulder prehab dose, and low-stance conditioning.

training_implications.implication: Track role-specific exposures: attack swings, serve attempts, jump sets, block jumps, approach jumps, hard dig reps, floor contacts, and minutes/rallies played. Pain trends should alter the next session before performance drops.
training_implications.backend_use: Create athlete-state checks that ask different load questions by role.

backend_records_to_create.role_summary: Primary offensive organizer who usually takes second contact, controls tempo, communicates plays, and converts pass quality into attack options.

serve_receive: avoid passing unless system or emergency requires it
communicate receive pattern and help-setter responsibility
offense: run quick, pin, and back-row options as skill allows
call for help when off balance
block: front-row right-side block responsibility in many systems
defense: defend assigned back-row or front-row zone
transition: move from defensive/base position to second-contact location

backend_records_to_create.role_summary: All-around left-side pin who commonly passes, attacks high and tempo sets, blocks the right-side threat, defends, and handles imperfect balls.

block: block opponent right-side or assigned pin
close with middle for double block
defense: dig cross-court or line by system
transition: convert pass/dig/block cover into attack readiness
handle high balls when team is out of system

backend_records_to_create.role_summary: Right-side attacker and blocker who balances the offense, often matches up with the opponent's outside hitter, and may be a major back-row attacking option.

offense: emergency attacking option when setter defends first contact
defense: cover setter if setter blocks or defends first ball

backend_records_to_create.role_summary: Central net player responsible for reading the pass and setter, controlling first-tempo threats, closing blocks to both pins, and attacking quick balls.

serve_receive: usually limited receive load after beginner level
prepare quick approach from receive pattern
offense: slide or gap option where used
defense: may be replaced by libero back row

backend_records_to_create.role_summary: Back-row defensive specialist with special replacement rules and attack/block restrictions who anchors serve receive, digging, floor leadership, and out-of-system ball control.

serve_receive: cover large court area when capable
offense: avoid illegal front-zone overhand set consequences
block: does not block or attempt block under FIVB rules
transition: set second ball if setter digs
reset team after chaotic first contact

backend_records_to_create.role_summary: Substitution-based back-row ball-control role used to improve serve receive, digging, serving, and defensive stability without using libero replacement rules.

serve_receive: enter to pass for a weaker receiver or front-row specialist
offense: possible legal back-row attack if trained
block: normally not a block role unless substitution pattern places player front row
defense: defend immediately after serving if applicable

backend_records_to_create.role_summary: Short-exposure substitution role used to create serve pressure, target a receiver, change serve type, or replace a weaker server.

serve_receive: not primary receive role unless also a DS
offense: emergency free-ball or second contact if rally continues
block: not primary block role unless remaining through front-row rotation
defense: recover from serve into defensive base
transition: sub out or continue based on rotation plan

beginner: learn simple 4-2 or beginner target rules
intermediate: set pins and middle from varied passes
advanced: manage hot hitter and weak blocker matchups

secondary: serve receive if system uses all-around opposite

intermediate: attack fast and high right-side sets
advanced: stress opponent receive/block with serve and attack

beginner: hands over net without net faults

intermediate: enter cold and pass under pressure
advanced: combine serve pressure with elite defense
vary serve by scouting and score state

backend_records_to_create.role_specific_notes: Setters need finger/hand tolerance for high set volume, shoulder endurance for repeated overhead contacts, and safe landing/blocking preparation if front row.
Outside hitters often stack receive, attack, block, and dig load, so swing count, jump count, and landing quality should be monitored together.
Opposites may have heavy attack and block load with less receive movement; protect shoulder, knee, ankle, and back as right-side power demands rise.
Middle blockers need careful progression of block jumps, quick attacks, lateral net movement, and hand/finger exposure because net-play density is high.
Liberos have lower jump load but high low-posture, dig, wrist/hand, dive, shoulder, hip, and low-back demands.
Defensive specialists share libero-like floor-defense risks and also need readiness routines because they may enter after sitting.
Serving specialists should not accumulate excessive serving volume just because their match role is short; quality and readiness matter more than bulk reps.

beginner: play all skills in simple systems

advanced: heavy receive and attack load management
